Because it accords with the time of grace that the Sacrament of communion and love should not merely signify communion and love, but also inflame unto the same; and because that which most inflames us to mutual love and…

Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you. But does it suffice for salvation to believe and to be baptized? No; rather, instruction in morals is also required; therefore he says teaching them…
n: *Bethphage *is a Hebrew name that means *house of figs. *It was probably on the east side of the Mount of Olives, between Bethany and Jerusalem.

For the first time in Matthew’s gospel, Jesus openly acted as Israel’s King and Messiah. He rode into Jerusalem in victory. But even in victory Jesus was gentle. He rode a donkey and not a war horse.

The crowds covered the road with their coats and with palm branches. These were common ways that Jews welcomed people and celebrated victory. The crowds also sang an important song from Psalm 118. This song was hundreds of years old. It’s about how God comes to save his people who are suffering. Singing it about Jesus meant that Jesus was God’s answer to his people’s troubles.

Jesus accepted being called the Son of David. This was a way of announcing that he is the King. Then with royal authority Jesus entered the temple. The temple wasn’t being used in a way that honoured God. Many people were using the temple to make money. They weren’t using it as a place of prayer. Jesus forced them to leave. Jesus made sure that it was once again used as a place of praise and healing.
Jesus entering Jerusalem starts Matthew's story of how the Messiah's suffering and resurrection establish salvation.
Jesus was revealing himself as the Lord who, as king of Israel, goes up to Mount Zion on a donkey ({{Matthew 21:5|Matthew 21:5}}; see {{Zechariah 9:9|Zechariah 9:9}}).

This part of the Old Testament fulfillment emphasizes the Messiah's peaceful, humble, and saving work (see {{Matthew 11:28-30|Matthew 11:28–30}}; {{Isaiah 62:11|Isaiah 62:11}}; {{Zechariah 9:9-10|Zechariah 9:9–10}}).

- The crowds with Jesus saw him as a prophet, empowered by God to teach and perform miracles. 

- The mention *from Nazareth in Galilee* emphasizes the humble beginnings of Jesus (see {{Matthew 2:23|Matthew 2:23}}).

- *Buying and selling* happened in the temple complex, in the Court of the Gentiles. 

- *Money changers* made profit by exchanging foreign money into the official Jewish currency. Jesus criticized this commercial activity because it dishonored the holiness of the temple (see {{Mark 11:11-18|Mark 11:11–18}}).

The close association of the temple cleansing (see {{John 2:13-16|John 2:13–16}}) and the cursing of the fig tree ({{Matthew 21:18-19|Matthew 21:18–19}}) shows Jesus as the Messiah (God’s chosen one). He confronted Israel and warned that God judges those who reject the Messiah and his message.
What Jesus did was right because people were using money in a way that desecrated God's glory.
The Jewish leaders’ refusal to believe is contrasted with the joyful faith and praise of little children (see {{Matthew 18:1-14|Matthew 18:1–14}}; {{Matthew 19:13-15|19:13–15}}).

*Have you never read:* Jesus asked this challenging question to opponents who failed to see that his ministry fulfilled the promises about the Messiah (see also {{Matthew 12:3|Matthew 12:3}}, {{Matthew 12:5|5}}; {{Matthew 19:4|19:4}}; {{Matthew 21:42|21:42}}; {{Matthew 22:31|22:31}}).

The next morning Jesus went back to Jerusalem. He was hungry.

The fig tree he saw had no fruit. The tree was a picture of God’s people in Jesus’ time. God wanted them to be like strong and healthy plants that produced a good harvest. But Israel didn’t bear the fruit of good works that God was looking for.

Jesus didn’t want things to stay the way they were in Israel. Over and over again he taught that God’s people must turn away from sin. They had to turn towards God and obey him only.

The things Jesus taught challenged the teachings of Israel’s elders. So the leaders challenged Jesus by questioning his authority. But Jesus kept teaching and working.

- *Nothing on it except leaves*: Mark notes that "it was not the season for figs" (see {{Mark 11:13|Mark 11:13}}). It was spring, just before Passover. Figs start growing in spring but ripen in fall. 

- *immediately the tree withered*: Matthew seems to have shortened the story (compare {{Matthew 21:18-22|Matthew 21:18–22}}; {{Mark 11:13-14|Mark 11:13–14}}, {{Mark 11:20-23|20–23}}). The cursing of the fig tree symbolizes God's judgment on Israel for rejecting the Messiah (see {{Matthew 3:9|Matt 3:9}}; {{Matthew 8:11-12|8:11–12}}). The Israelites are like a fig tree that looks promising but has no fruit. This was especially true of the hypocritical leaders. They did not *bear fruit*, symbolic of receiving the Messiah (see {{Matthew 21:33-46|21:33–46}}).
Jesus was encouraging the disciples to trust in God and pray with faith. He was not promising that God would approve everything they might desire ({{1 John 5:14-15|1 John 5:14–15}}).

*Elders of the people:* This refers to the family leaders from each tribe. They were part of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council in Jerusalem (compare {{Ezra 5:5|Ezra 5:5}}; {{Ezra 6:14|6:14}}; {{Ezra 10:8|10:8}}).

This section focuses on how Jewish leaders challenged the authority of Jesus. Each time, the wisdom of Jesus revealed their lack of spiritual understanding. These debates also revealed the status of Jesus as the Messiah and the consequences of rejecting him. Sadly, the leaders became more resistant with each encounter and plotted to kill Jesus ({{Matthew 21:23|Matthew 21:23}}, {{Matthew 21:46|46}}; {{Matthew 22:15-17|22:15–17}}, {{Matthew 22:23|23}}, {{Matthew 22:34|34}}, {{Matthew 22:41|41}}).

Jesus gave a riddle. The answer solved the leaders’ question and placed them in a dilemma that showed what was in their hearts ({{Matthew 21:25-26|Matthew 21:25–26}}). Asking a counter-question was common in debates at that time.

The minsitry of John, like the ministry of Jesus, was controversial (see {{Matthew 3:1|Matthew 3:1}}, {{Matthew 3:5-6|5–6}}). This was true especially after John publicly criticized Herod Antipas for his sins (see {{Matthew 14:4|14:4}}). The Jewish leaders did not want to admit that John's work was from God. They had refused to believe John and repent of their sins ({{Matthew 3:2|3:2}}). They also refused to accept Jesus as the Messiah ({{John 1:29-34|John 1:29–34}}).
The Jewish leaders did not have the honesty or bravery to admit their beliefs about John. So, it was fair for Jesus not to answer their question.
This parable continues to emphasize why John is important.

Jesus told two stories that talked about Israel as God’s vineyard. Many people who said yes to Jesus were like the first son in the first story. This included tax collectors, prostitutes, outsiders and people who were hated by others.

Israel’s leaders were like the second son in the story. They said that they would obey God but they didn’t. In the next story, God cared for his vineyard with much love and attention. He expected to find good grapes. Jesus was talking about how people should act when they have turned away from sin. The good harvest should be shown in the lives of those who trust God and obey him. But Israel’s leaders didn’t share any of the harvest with God. They were the tenants in the story who killed God’s servants and his Son. So they couldn’t stay in the vineyard.

The religious leaders were very angry when they heard this story. Jesus once again used words from Psalm 118. This part of the psalm is about an important stone. The builders didn’t want to use it in what they were making. Yet the stone was used. It became the most important stone in the building. The religious leaders were like those builders. Jesus was like the stone. Many of God’s people were refusing to accept him. Yet Jesus would become the most important part of the kingdom God was building.
Three parables expose the guilt of those who rejected the Messiah and lost their special status as God's chosen people. God now considers only those who accept Jesus as the Messiah as his people.
*I will not*: This response must have offended Jews who learned from a young age to show respect for the authority of a father (see {{Matthew 8:21-22|Matthew 8:21–22}}).
The right way to live is to follow the will of God ({{Matthew 3:15|Matthew 3:15}}; {{Matthew 5:20|5:20}}; see also {{Proverbs 8:20|Proverbs 8:20}}; {{Proverbs 12:28|12:28}}).

In this story, Jesus refers back to {{Isaiah 5:1-7|Isaiah 5:1–7}}. The people of Israel who rejected God's Messiah lost the privilege of being God's people. Now, God has called the Christian community, made up of both Jews and Gentiles (non-Jews), to be his people (see {{Romans 9:4-8|Romans 9:4–8}}; {{Romans 11:1-12|11:1–12}}).

*He sent his servants*: The prophets had spoken God's message to Israel. In this parable, the tenant farmers represent Israel's leaders, whom Jesus blamed for killing God's prophets ({{Matthew 23:29-37|Matthew 23:29–37}}).
*Finally*: God's revelation reached its goal in Jesus (see {{Matthew 13:16-17|Matthew 13:16–17}}; {{Hebrews 1:1-2|Hebrews 1:1–2}}).
*when the owner of the vineyard returns: *The vineyard owner's return symbolizes the Lord's coming for judgment (see {{Matthew 16:27|Matthew 16:27}}; {{Matthew 24:1-36|24:1–36}}).
The Jewish religious leaders declared their own condemnation.

*The cornerstone* was either the first stone of the foundation or the last stone placed, like the top of an arch. The builders rejected this stone as unworthy, but it was actually the most important. Jesus was talking about his role in the kingdom of God ({{Matthew 21:43|Matthew 21:43}}) and how the Jewish religious leaders rejected him.

- *Taken away from you*: Either the privilege of being God’s chosen nation no longer belonged to the Jews, or the religious leaders had lost the privilege of being leaders of God’s people (see {{Romans 9:1-11:36|Romans 9–11}}). 

- The Christian community is a nation that will produce the proper "fruit" or right results. This means a life of trust and obedience that shows the start of God's kingdom (see {{Matthew 3:8|Matthew 3:8}}; {{Matthew 7:15-20|7:15–20}}; {{Matthew 12:33|12:33}}; {{Matthew 13:8|13:8}}, {{Matthew 13:26|26}}).

Those who opposed the Messiah would soon win a temporary victory. But the Messiah would eventually defeat them. The *stone* would crush them because the death of Jesus on the cross led to his vindication and triumph (see also {{Daniel 2:34-35|Daniel 2:34–35}}, {{Daniel 2:44-45|44–45}}).
This explanation fits with Matthew’s theme of God’s judgment on the Jewish leaders who misled the people of Israel (see {{Matthew 23:13-15|Matthew 23:13–15}}).

In Jesus’ time people often spoke about God’s kingdom like a great feast. Jesus told a story about that.

The story was about how God had invited Israel into the kingdom of heaven. But they refused to be part of it. They made this clear by refusing to follow God’s ways.

God sent many prophets to give them warnings. They treated the prophets badly. Then they wouldn’t accept Jesus as the King’s own Son. Because of these things, Israel would face terrible judgement.

Judgement came in the year AD 70 when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem.

In the story Jesus told, other people were invited into God’s kingdom instead. All who follow God’s ways will be God’s guests at his great feast.

In this parable, Israel had often rejected God’s message in the past. In the same way, Israel rejected the Messiah and faced judgment. In Israel’s place, God raised up the church ({{Matthew 16:17-19|Matthew 16:17–19}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}). God also expects the church to live in righteousness ({{Romans 11:11-24|Romans 11:11–24}}).

- The *king* represents God, and *his son* is Jesus ({{Galatians 4:4|Galatians 4:4}}; {{Hebrews 1:1-2|Hebrews 1:1–2}}). 

- The feast represents the kingdom of the Messiah.
*those he had invited: *This refers to the nation of Israel. They ignored God's servants, the prophets (see study note on Matthew 21:33–46).
Jesus was referring to the future destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 (see {{Matthew 23:37-39|Matthew 23:37–39}}; {{Matthew 24:2|24:2}}).
People who refuse God's invitation do not deserve to enter his kingdom (see {{Matthew 3:8|Matthew 3:8}}; {{Matthew 10:13|10:13}}, {{Matthew 10:37-38|37–38}}).

*as many as you can find*: God's invitation is now open to all people, not only the nation of Israel (see {{Matthew 28:16-20|Matthew 28:16–20}}; compare {{Matthew 10:5-6|10:5–6}}; {{Matthew 15:21-28|15:21–28}}).
Wearing the right clothes symbolizes spiritual qualities that show true faith (see {{Matthew 7:13-27|Matthew 7:13–27}}).

- *weeping and gnashing of teeth: *This phrase describes the intense pain and sorrow that come from being condemned for sin and unbelief (see {{Matthew 8:12|Matthew 8:12}}; {{Matthew 13:42|13:42}}, {{Matthew 13:50|50}}; {{Matthew 24:51|24:51}}; {{Matthew 25:30|25:30}}). 

- *outer darkness: *This is a picture of eternal punishment, shown as being far from God’s presence.
Many people receive an invitation to the kingdom. But God only choses a few who faithfully obey Jesus.
In first-century Palestine, debates about Roman taxes were intense (see also {{Matthew 17:24-27|Matthew 17:24–27}}).

The Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees usually disagreed with one another and fought for power. But they all worked together against Jesus.

Jesus wasn’t part of any of Israel’s groups of leaders. He didn’t teach the same things that Israel’s elders had taught for hundreds of years. He spoke fresh and powerful words that showed what God’s kingdom is like.

The Pharisees and Herodians tried to trap Jesus by asking a hard question. Their question was about whether to obey a human government or God. But Jesus didn’t allow them to trap him. Instead he gave them a wise answer. People under Caesar’s authority must obey Caesar. But people must be more faithful to God than to any government.

Then the Sadducees tried to trap Jesus with a difficult story. They didn’t believe that people would rise from the dead. Jesus corrected them. He showed that the resurrection wouldn't be like what they were thinking. The bodies of people raised from the dead won’t be exactly like bodies are now. What really matters is that God is the powerful God of life.

The Pharisees were strict Jewish leaders who opposed Roman rule. They strongly resisted Roman control and wanted to protect Jewish traditions and independence. They usually disagreed with the supporters of Herod. But in this case, they joined together because both groups hated Jesus.

*Is it lawful … or not?*: They asked the question to try and trap Jesus. If he said no, they could arrest him for rebelling against Rome. If he said yes, they could accuse him of supporting Roman oppression.

The people had to pay the poll tax with the denarius coin. This coin showed the picture and title of Caesar (the Roman emperor). Old Testament rules against worshiping images ({{Exodus 20:4|Exodus 20:4}}; {{Leviticus 26:1|Leviticus 26:1}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:15-24|Deuteronomy 4:15–24}}) made this coin controversial for Jews (see Josephus, *War* 2.9.2–3). To avoid conflict, some Roman governors in Palestine minted coins without human images. This showed respect for Jewish religious concerns.

Jesus answered with wisdom. He said people should give Caesar the honor that belongs to him, but they must give God the greater honor and loyalty. Being loyal to God does not always mean being disloyal to human rulers. Jesus showed that there are two realms of authority, Caesar’s and God’s, and God’s authority is greater ({{Acts 4:19|Acts 4:19}}).

The* Sadducees *(see {{Matthew 3:7|Matthew 3:7}}) described a situation about *levirate* marriage. This was a Jewish custom where a man marries his brother's widow (see {{Genesis 38:6-11|Genesis 38:6–11}}; {{Deuteronomy 25:5-6|Deuteronomy 25:5–6}}). They tried to use this as proof that resurrection from the dead is impossible.
The *resurrection* was an important topic in the time of Jesus. But the people only asked about it to try and trap him.
*the power of God:* This probably means God's ability to resurrect people who have died.

*like the angels in heaven*: Jesus was not teaching that people will be without gender in heaven. Nor was he criticizing God's order of marriage and sexuality. Instead, he was confirming that God will transform people into a glorious new existence (see {{1 Corinthians 15:35-49|1 Corinthians 15:35–49}}; {{2 Corinthians 5:1-5|2 Corinthians 5:1–5}}). In this new existence, parts of the current world, like marriage, will not be present.
God spoke of himself as the God of Abraham in the present tense. This shows that Abraham is still alive and that there will be a resurrection.

The Pharisees tried one last time to argue against Jesus and win. They asked him what the most important commandment was. Jesus gave answers that most Jews in Israel at the time would have agreed with.

The first important commandment was to be completely faithful to God and serve only him. The words Jesus used came from the Shema.

The second important commandment was to take care of their neighbours. Then Jesus asked the Pharisees a hard question. How can the Messiah be both David’s son and David’s Lord? This was a mystery about Jesus that Israel’s leaders never understood. They couldn’t accept that God had come to earth in a human body. They were confused and didn’t know how to answer. The leaders stopped trying to trap Jesus with words.
Many strict Jews believed that every commandment was equally important. Because of this, a careless answer to the question could lead to an accusation of rejecting God’s law.

Jesus answers using the Shema ({{Deuteronomy 6:4-9|Deuteronomy 6:4–9}}), a key statement of God's covenant with Israel. The first Hebrew word in {{Deuteronomy 6:4-9|Deuteronomy 6:4–9}} is *shema*‘, meaning "hear!"
*Love your neighbor as yourself*: {{Leviticus 19:18|Leviticus 19:18}}; see also {{Romans 13:9|Romans 13:9}}; {{Galatians 5:6|Galatians 5:6}}, {{Galatians 5:14|14}}; {{James 2:8|James 2:8}}.
*hang on*: The words of Jesus showed that God’s will is unified and consistent, as it is recorded in Scripture.

After Jesus defended himself against the traps of his opponents ({{Matthew 21:23-22:40|21:23–22:40}}), he asked them a question. How can the Messiah be called both the *son of David* and also the *Lord of David *({{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}).

*Whose son is He? … David's*: See study note on Matthew 9:27; also see {{2 Samuel 7:12-14|2 Samuel 7:12–14}}; {{Psalm 2:7-9|Psalms 2:7–9}}; {{Psalm 110:1-7|110}}; {{Isaiah 11:1|Isaiah 11:1}}, {{Isaiah 11:10|10}}; {{Jeremiah 23:5-6|Jeremiah 23:5–6}}.

The quote is from {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}} and New Testament writers often use it to describe Jesus (see {{Acts 2:34-35|Acts 2:34–35}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:25|1 Corinthians 15:25}}; {{Hebrews 1:13|Hebrews 1:13}}; {{Hebrews 2:8|2:8}}; {{Hebrews 10:12-13|10:12–13}}; {{Revelation 3:21|Revelation 3:21}}).
*how can He be David’s son?:* The answer is that Jesus is not only the son of David; he is also the Son of God ({{Matthew 14:33|Matthew 14:33}}).
No one could answer him because they had never thought the Messiah would be God as a human being in the flesh (see {{John 1:1-14|John 1:1–14}}).

The Jewish religious leaders tried to find a reason to accuse Jesus publicly but could not ({{Matthew 21:23-22:46|Matthew 21:23–22:46}}). Jesus then addressed the crowds and his disciples to openly criticize the religious leaders for often failing to obey God's righteous standards.

Jesus spoke words of judgement against a group of Israel’s leaders. The teachers of the law and the Pharisees sat in the seat of Moses. This meant they had authority to teach the people like Moses did. But this group of Israel’s leaders were pretenders.

On the outside they looked clean and holy. Yet on the inside they were full of sin and hatred. They cared about looking powerful and important. They didn’t really care about helping the people they led.

Seven times Jesus warned them how terrible the judgement against them would be. This group of religious leaders refused to accept Jesus. This made Jesus very sad.

He longed to take care of God’s people like a hen protects her baby chicks. But the leaders didn’t want Jesus to share God’s tender love with people.
This last extended teaching (see study note on Matthew 5:1–7:29) focuses on the judgment awaiting those who reject the Messiah.

*The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat:* This means that they give authoritative explanations about the law of Moses. They passed down oral traditions associated with the law and thought to be from Moses. They judged religious and social issues based on these traditions (see {{Matthew 15:2|Matthew 15:2}}).

*practice and obey:* This was not a full confirmation of everything the Pharisees taught (see {{Matthew 15:1-20|Matthew 15:1–20}}; {{Matthew 16:5-12|16:5–12}}; {{Matthew 23:13-39|23:13–39}}). It might refer only to teachings that agreed with the law of Moses, or it could be bitter irony or sarcasm. Jesus might also have advised conforming to the Pharisees’ teachings to avoid causing offense ({{Matthew 17:24-27|17:24–27}}).

- *heavy, burdensome loads:* According to the rabbis, there were 613 laws with commands and prohibitions (see {{Matthew 11:28-30|11:28–30}}; {{Acts 15:10|Acts 15:10}}, {{Acts 15:28|28}}). 

- *not willing to lift a finger:* The religious leaders were not willing to ease or change these traditional laws.

- *phylacteries*: Pious Jews sometimes wore small prayer boxes, called phylacteries. These were placed on the head and the upper left arm. Inside were written copies of important Old Testament commands (see {{Deuteronomy 6:6-9|Deuteronomy 6:6–9}}; {{Deuteronomy 11:18-19|11:18–19}}). 

- Another custom was wearing *tassels*, which were also a sign of devotion (see {{Matthew 9:20|Matthew 9:20}}; see also {{Numbers 15:38-41|Numbers 15:38–41}}). Some made their tassels extra long to draw attention to their religious devotion.
*the chief seats in the synagogue:* These were close to the Torah scrolls and faced the congregation.
*Rabbi* was a title given to an authoritative and respected Jewish teacher.

*Rabbi:* In Judaism, these men were authoritative mediators for sharing knowledge about God (see {{Matthew 23:7|Matthew 23:7}}). But under the new covenant, there is only one authoritative teacher, Jesus himself as the Messiah (see {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31–34}}).

Jesus does not forbid using titles (especially for one's father). Instead, he warns against claiming undue honor when teaching about God. In the community of Jesus, everyone is equal and knows God (see {{Matthew 12:46-50|12:46–50}}; {{Matthew 18:15-20|18:15–20}}). The titles *Rabbi, Father*, and *Teacher* are similar in meaning.

- Later Jewish writings show that people respected teachers by calling them *Father* (see, for example, *Mishnah Eduyyoth* {{Matthew 1:4|1:4}}). 

- *one Father*: See {{Matthew 6:9|Matthew 6:9}}; {{Malachi 2:10|Malachi 2:10}}; compare {{1 Corinthians 4:15|1 Corinthians 4:15}}.
*Instructor:* This title means the role and office of guiding others to understand God. Jesus, not the scribes and Pharisees, is the teacher of God's will ({{Matthew 5:17|Matthew 5:17}}).
The disciples of Jesus should lead by serving others, in distinct contrast to Israel's religious leaders (described in {{Matthew 23:5-7|23:5–7}}).

- *Woe to you: *This is a distinct warning about God's judgment. 

- *hypocrites!*: In English, hypocrisy means a contradiction between what is real and what seems to be real. In the Bible, it means misunderstanding God's will, misleading others, and facing God's judgment. This often includes: desire for fame and power ({{Matthew 23:5-12|Matthew 23:5–12}}), misuse of teaching authority, false teachings ({{Matthew 23:13-22|23:13–22}}), and focusing on minor ethical details ({{Matthew 23:23-28|23:23–28}}).

A suitable English word for these behaviors is *heresy*. The Pharisees and religious teachers showed these traits. As the Christian church grew, these traits continued to appear (for example, {{1 Timothy 4:1-3|1 Timothy 4:1–3}}; {{2 Peter 2:1-22|2 Peter 2:1–22}}). So God's children must always be on guard against them ({{James 4:7-10|James 4:7–10}}; {{1 Peter 2:1-3|1 Peter 2:1–3}}). 

- *you shut the kingdom:* This comes through their false teachings and opposition to Jesus (see {{Matthew 9:32-34|Matthew 9:32–34}}; {{Matthew 12:22-37|12:22–37}}; {{Matthew 15:12-14|15:12–14}}; {{Matthew 21:15|21:15}}; {{John 9:13-34|John 9:13–34}}). The Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees stopped others from hearing and believing the truth about the Messiah.

Matthew gathered seven warnings of sorrow to come (literally *woe to you*) inspired by similar Old Testament lists ({{Isaiah 5:8-23|Isaiah 5:8–23}}; {{Habakkuk 2:6-20|Habakkuk 2:6–20}}). Matthew arranged them to reach a climax with the killing of the prophets.

- A* convert* (*proselyte*) fully accepted Judaism by performing ceremonies like baptism, sacrifice, and circumcision (see {{Acts 13:43|Acts 13:43}}). 

A *convert *differed from a "God-fearer." A God-fearer was a person who accepted some Jewish beliefs, especially monotheism (belief in one God), without fully converting to Judaism (see {{Luke 7:4-5|Luke 7:4–5}}; {{Acts 10:2|Acts 10:2}}). *To win a single convert *likely means persuading God-fearers to fully convert by becoming circumcised (compare {{Galatians 2:3|Galatians 2:3}}, {{Galatians 2:14|14}}; {{Matthew 5:2-12|5:2–12}}; {{Matthew 6:12-13|6:12–13}}). 

- *of hell*: The Greek word here is *Gehenna*. It was a valley outside Jerusalem used as a place of burning; See study note on Matthew 5:29.

The religious leaders said that some oaths were less binding, and this allowed them to deceive people. But Jesus called for honesty and for keeping every commitment (see {{Matthew 5:33-37|Matthew 5:33–37}}).

The Jewish teachers of religious law and Pharisees believed that careful and precise tithing showed their dedication to the law. Without denying the importance of tithing, Jesus revealed that they completely ignored the more important parts of the law ({{Isaiah 1:16-17|Isaiah 1:16–17}}; {{Jeremiah 22:3|Jeremiah 22:3}}; {{Hosea 6:6|Hosea 6:6}}; {{Micah 6:8|Micah 6:8}}; {{Zechariah 7:9|Zechariah 7:9}}).

*gnat … camel:* In Aramaic, the language Jesus likely spoke, these two words sound similar (*qalma* … *gamla*). This makes a wordplay or pun. Jesus used the contrast between a tiny gnat and a huge camel to show the hypocrisy of focusing on small details while ignoring much greater issues.

If a person is pure inside, it leads to doing the right things. But doing the right things does not make a person pure inside ({{Matthew 6:19-34|Matthew 6:19–34}}; {{Matthew 12:33-37|12:33–37}}; {{Matthew 15:15-20|15:15–20}}).

Jewish people used to coat limestone tombs, like funerary urns or ossuaries, with a mixture of marble and lime. This filled the holes and made the tombs look nicer. It also helped visitors to Jerusalem see and avoid them, preventing contamination. Jesus did not criticize decorating tombs. Instead, he compared these whitewashed tombs to Jewish religious teachers and Pharisees. Both looked good on the outside but had contamination and impurity on the inside.

By building and decorating the tombs for the prophets, the teachers of religious law and Pharisees showed outward support for the prophets. But inwardly they were of the same sinful character as their ancestors who had murdered the prophets.

*Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers*: By killing God's Messiah, they would complete Israel's history of killing God's prophets (see {{1 Thessalonians 2:14-16|1 Thessalonians 2:14–16}}).

This covers the first and last murders recorded in the Hebrew Bible. Abel was killed in {{Genesis 4:8-11|Genesis 4:8–11}}, and Zechariah in {{2 Chronicles 24:15-22|2 Chronicles 24:15–22}}, which is the last book in the Hebrew Bible order. Jesus implies that his generation would be held guilty for all the murders of God’s righteous servants in the Old Testament (compare {{Matthew 27:25|Matt 27:25}}).

- Even though Jesus had just given a severe judgment against Israel ({{Matthew 23:29-36|Matthew 23:29–36}}), he truly wanted them to repent and accept God's grace. 

- *as a hen:* This is an image of protective care (see also {{Deuteronomy 32:11|Deuteronomy 32:11}}; {{Ruth 2:12|Ruth 2:12}}; {{Psalm 17:8|Psalms 17:8}}; {{Psalm 36:7|36:7}}; {{Psalm 57:1|57:1}}; {{Psalm 61:4|61:4}}; {{Psalm 91:4|91:4}}).

*your house is left to you desolate:* God would leave the temple ({{Ezekiel 10:18-19|Ezekiel 10:18–19}}; {{Ezekiel 11:22-23|11:22–23}}; compare {{Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23}}). Then God would allow the destruction of both the temple and Jerusalem.
*Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord:* his may point to a future time when the nation of Israel will turn to the Messiah (see also {{Romans 11:12-32|Romans 11:12–32}}).
The architecture of the temple was a source of pride for the Jewish people (see study note on Mark 13:1).

Jesus’ disciples were amazed by the greatness of the temple buildings. Jesus replied with a prophecy that shocked them. The temple would be destroyed.

This was the start of Jesus’ fifth long message. He spoke it while he and the disciples were on the Mount of Olives. Jesus answered the disciples’ questions using words from Isaiah 19:2. He said that the beginning of these events would be like birth-pains.

The troubles Jesus described had to do with God’s plan to make the world new again. Before a new baby arrives, there is pain and suffering for the mother. It would be like that before God’s kingdom comes.

Much of the suffering Jesus described happened right after he was raised from the dead. It happened to his followers in the years AD 30 to 70. They were treated badly as they preached the good news of Jesus’ kingdom. The book of Acts talks about this.

Some think chapter {{Matthew 24:1-51|24}} is about the return of Jesus at the end of time. Others think it as a prediction of events in AD 70, when the Romans destroyed Jerusalem and the temple. Some think it refers to both events. See also study notes on Mark 13.

*not one stone: *The destruction of Jerusalem and the temple showed God's judgment against Israel (see {{1 Kings 9:7-9|1 Kings 9:7–9}}; {{Jeremiah 7:8-15|Jeremiah 7:8–15}}; {{Jeremiah 9:10-12|9:10–12}}; {{Jeremiah 26:6|26:6}}, {{Jeremiah 26:18|18}}; {{Micah 3:12|Micah 3:12}}; see also {{Isaiah 64:11|Isaiah 64:11}}; {{Luke 19:44|Luke 19:44}}; {{Acts 6:14|Acts 6:14}}).

- The Greek word *parousia* means *coming* or *appearing*. 

- *end of the age *(or *end of the world*): This phrase refers to the final end of a period in salvation history (see {{Matthew 13:39-40|Matthew 13:39–40}}, {{Matthew 13:49|49}}; also {{Hebrews 9:26|Hebrews 9:26}}). The second coming of Jesus will end normal history with a final judgment. The disciples believed the temple's destruction and the end of history had a close link.

Jesus warned his disciples not to be tricked by false messiahs and not to lose hope when disasters come. These things do not mean the end has come right away. History must follow the course God has set. The signs in {{Matthew 24:4-8|Matthew 24:4–8}} are not the end themselves but events that come before the end.

*claiming, ‘I am the Christ,’: *During AD 30 to 70, many false prophets and miracle workers claimed to be the Messiah. They convinced people to follow them, promising salvation (Josephus, *Antiquities* 18.4.1; 20.5.1; 20.8.6; *War* 6.5.2). The first known person to openly claim to be the Messiah was Bar Kochba in AD 132. It is unclear if Jesus was talking about impostors before the temple's destruction, false messiahs throughout the church Age, or possibly during a future difficult time.

- *These things must happen:* This shows that times of trouble are part of God’s plan as he moves history toward its conclusion (see {{Matthew 24:7|Matthew 24:7}}, {{Matthew 24:29-30|29–30}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:8-12|2 Thessalonians 2:8–12}}). 

- *the end*: This might mean the end of a period (like in AD 70) or the end of human history as we know it (compare {{Matthew 24:13-14|Matthew 24:13–14}}; see also {{Matthew 10:22|10:22}}; {{Matthew 13:39-40|13:39–40}}, {{Matthew 13:49|49}}).

*beginning of birth pains:* God's people should expect intense suffering right before the second coming of Jesus (see also {{Matthew 24:29-31|Mathhew 24:29–31}}; {{Isaiah 13:8|Isaiah 13:8}}; {{Isaiah 26:17|26:17}}; {{Jeremiah 4:31|Jeremiah 4:31}}; {{Jeremiah 6:24|6:24}}; {{Micah 4:9-10|Micah 4:9–10}}).

*hated *(see {{Acts 28:22|Acts 28:22}}): At the end of the first century, the Roman historian Tacitus described Christians as “the hated ones of mankind” (Tacitus, *Annals* 15.44). The suffering of righteous people sometimes has the purpose of encouraging repentance and obedience (see {{Exodus 4:31|Exodus 4:31}}; {{Deuteronomy 4:30|Deuteronomy 4:30}}; {{Judges 10:6-16|Judges 10:6–16}}; {{Psalm 34:19|Psalms 34:19}}; {{Psalm 37:39|37:39}}; {{Psalm 50:15|50:15}}).
Some people will stop being loyal to Jesus because of persecution ({{Matthew 10:25|Matthew 10:25}}; {{Matthew 13:21|13:21}}; {{Matthew 16:24-28|16:24–28}}; {{Matthew 26:33|26:33}}).
*the love of most will grow cold* (see {{Revelation 2:4|Revelation 2:4}}): If the love within the community of the disciples of Jesus disappears, the community stops being what God designed it to be.
*the one who perseveres *stays loyal to Jesus, even when persecuted. *The end* could mean the end of their life, the judgment on Israel in AD 70, or the end of history.

- *in all the world:* This points to the future mission to the Gentiles (see {{Matthew 21:43|Matthew 21:43}}; {{Matthew 28:16-20|28:16–20}}). Before the end comes, there will be a time, whether short or long, when the good news spreads among the nations.

- Jesus said the end will be marked by three signs. First is "the abomination of desolation" ({{Matthew 24:15|24:15}}). Second is severe persecution ({{Matthew 24:16-28|24:16–28}}). Finally comes the sign of the Son of Man ({{Matthew 24:29-31|24:29–31}}).

- *described by the prophet Daniel*: He spoke about the desecration (or *desolation*) of the temple (see {{Daniel 8:13|Daniel 8:13}}; {{Daniel 9:27|9:27}}; {{Daniel 11:31|11:31}}; {{Daniel 12:11|12:11}}). It would be made unclean and ruined.

- *the abomination of desolation* could be: 

- A false priest taking over the priesthood (see Josephus, *War* 4.3.6–10).

- Unlawful images of God or humans, or certain people who cannot be in the temple. These people would include Antiochus Epiphanes, Caligula, Vespasian, or Titus (see Josephus, *War* 4.4.1–4.7.1).

- The antichrist being present in the temple (compare *1 Maccabees* 1:54–64; *2 Maccabees* 8:17). The term "antichrist" refers to a person or teaching that opposes Jesus Christ and his work.

- *let the reader understand:* This hidden message shows a special connection between the writer and reader, based on a shared belief that these events fulfill the prophecies of {{Daniel 9:1-27|Daniel 9}}, {{Daniel 11:1-45|11}}, and {{Daniel 12:1-13|12}}.

Jesus said that the troubles in Israel would happen while his disciples were still alive. His words came true in the years AD 66 to AD 70. The Romans used the temple in ways that weren’t holy and then destroyed the temple.

Jesus talked about himself as the Son of Man. He fulfilled the prophet Daniel’s vision about the ruler whose kingdom would never be destroyed (Daniel 7:13–14).

Only God knows exactly when Jesus will come back to earth. Only God knows when everyone will see that Jesus is the true King. Jesus didn’t want his followers to be surprised by it or worried about missing it. His faithful followers can live every day with hope knowing that Jesus’ return will happen.

- The Jewish historian Josephus records that the Jordan River swells in winter, making it harder to cross (see *War* 4.7.5). Muddy roads also made travel difficult in winter. 

- Jews usually did not travel on the Sabbath, so that they could rest as God commanded (see {{Genesis 2:1-3|Genesis 2:1–3}}; {{Exodus 20:8-11|Exodus 20:8–11}}; {{Exodus 23:12|23:12}}; {{Exodus 31:12-17|31:12–17}}; {{Leviticus 23:3|Leviticus 23:3}}; {{Deuteronomy 5:12-15|Deuteronomy 5:12–15}}; {{Jeremiah 17:19-27|Jeremiah 17:19–27}}).

*great tribulation, unmatched:* Similar language appears in {{Nehemiah 9:37|Nehemiah 9:37}}; {{Jeremiah 11:16|Jeremiah 11:16}}; {{Daniel 12:1|Daniel 12:1}}; {{Joel 2:1-17|Joel 2:1–17}}. The Jewish historian Josephus documented the extreme violence of the times (see *War* 5.10.2–3).
God's chosen people persevere ({{Matthew 24:13|Matthew 24:13}}) and remain faithful ({{Matthew 24:37-25:46|24:37–25:46}}; see {{Isaiah 65:8-9|Isaiah 65:8–9}}; {{Romans 11:7|Romans 11:7}}).

- *false Christs and false prophets *(see {{Matthew 7:15|Matthew 7:15}}; {{Matthew 24:4-8|24:4–8}}; also {{Acts 13:6|Acts 13:6}}; {{2 Peter 2:1|2 Peter 2:1}}; {{1 John 2:18|1 John 2:18}}; {{1 John 4:1|4:1}}): Revelation describes a particular false prophet (see {{Revelation 16:13|Revelation 16:13}}). 

- *signs and wonders: *Not all miracles are proof of God's approval (see {{Deuteronomy 13:1-4|Deuteronomy 13:1–4}}; {{Revelation 13:13|Revelation 13:13}}).

- Some Jewish prophets persuaded people to follow them into the desert to witness signs of salvation (see {{Matthew 24:4-8|Matthew 24:4–8}}). 

- *in the inner rooms:* This might refer to secretive groups, like those at Qumran, or small fellowship groups linked to the Pharisees.
These verses expand on {{Matthew 24:23|Matthew 24:23}}. Jews debated where and how the Messiah would appear. The Messiah's glorious arrival and vindication will be clear to everyone.

*Lightning* here may point to the great cosmic signs that will mark the coming of the Messiah (see {{Matthew 24:29-31|Matthew 24:29–31}}; {{1 Thessalonians 4:13-18|1 Thessalonians 4:13–18}}). The focus is on how easy the *lightning *is to see, not how suddenly it comes. Jesus probably shared these teachings to prevent early excitement about the end of time ({{1 Thessalonians 4:13-5:10|1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:10}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:1-12|2 Thessalonians 2:1–12}}).

*‘The sun will be darkened … the heavens will be shaken.’:* This could be literal, as is fitting for a dramatic revelation of God's Son. Or, it could be a metaphor for a major cosmic event (see {{Acts 2:17-21|Acts 2:17–21}}; {{Hebrews 12:26-27|Hebrews 12:26–27}}; {{2 Peter 3:10|2 Peter 3:10}}; {{Revelation 6:12-13|Revelation 6:12–13}}). The Old Testament often uses similar apocalyptic language to describe political disasters and the collapse of governments as cosmic judgments from God (for example, {{Isaiah 13:9-16|Isaiah 13:9–16}}; {{Ezekiel 32:1-10|Ezekiel 32:1–10}}; {{Joel 2:1-17|Joel 2:1–17}}; {{Amos 8:7-10|Amos 8:7–10}}).

These sayings indicate the most important part of the discussion and answer the second question the disciples asked (see {{Matthew 24:3|Matthew 24:3}}). Some believe {{Matthew 24:29-31|24:29–31}} describes God's judgment on the Jewish people in AD 70. In this view, the apocalyptic images and metaphors picture the destruction of Jerusalem.

Others see these verses as pointing to the second coming of Christ at the end of history.

- *the sign of the Son of Man:* The sign is probably the Son of Man himself (see {{Matthew 12:38-42|Matthew 12:38–42}}; {{Matthew 16:4|16:4}}). His coming shows that God has vindicated him (proved him right; see {{Matthew 26:64|26:64}}). It will also cause deep mourning for those who face God’s judgment.

- *all the tribes of the earth:* This could also mean "all the tribes of the land." The Greek term used here (*phulai*) often refers to the tribes of Israel. It is not the usual term for Gentiles (*ethnoi*). This suggests that it may refer to a national disaster in Israel (see {{Matthew 21:43|Matthew 21:43}}; {{Zechariah 12:10-14|Zechariah 12:10–14}}). 

- *the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven*: See {{Daniel 7:13|Daniel 7:13}}. Many think this means the Son of Man will descend from God's presence to live on earth as judge and savior. This is the second coming of Christ. Others believe it describes the Son of Man coming in judgment, but not necessarily as the second coming of Christ (see {{Matthew 10:23|Matthew 10:23}}; {{Matthew 16:27|16:27}}; {{Matthew 19:28|19:28}}; {{Matthew 25:31|25:31}}; {{Matthew 26:64|26:64}}; {{Matthew 28:18|28:18}}).

Some believe this passage predicts the rapture, when God’s people are gathered by angels ({{Matthew 13:41|Matthew 13:41}}; {{Matthew 16:27|16:27}}; {{Matthew 25:31|25:31}}). Others think the word *angeloi* (Greek for “messengers”) here refers to human messengers ({{Matthew 11:10|11:10}}; {{Luke 7:24|Luke 7:24}}; {{Luke 9:52|9:52}}; {{James 2:25|James 2:25}}). In this view, Jesus is describing the spread of the good news among the Gentiles (see {{Matthew 21:33-46|Matthew 21:33–46}}; {{Matthew 22:1-14|22:1–14}}; {{Deuteronomy 30:1-10|Deuteronomy 30:1–10}}; {{Isaiah 27:13|Isaiah 27:13}}; {{Zechariah 2:6-13|Zechariah 2:6–13}}).

- *all these things:* This refers to events connected to the destruction of the temple. This phrase is first used in {{Matthew 23:36|Matthew 23:36}} (see {{Matthew 24:2|24:2}}, {{Matthew 24:8|8}}). 

- *He is near* (or *it is near*): It could mean the return of Jesus (see {{James 5:9|James 5:9}}; {{Revelation 3:20|Revelation 3:20}}), the destruction of the temple, or the end of history (see {{Luke 21:31|Luke 21:31}}).

*this generation:* In Matthew, *generation* refers particularly to the current Jews who do not trust in Jesus. This focuses especially on the leaders who have tried to make the people reject the Messiah ({{Matthew 11:16|Matthew 11:16}}; {{Matthew 12:39|12:39}}, {{Matthew 12:41-42|41–42}}, {{Matthew 12:45|45}}; {{Matthew 16:4|16:4}}; {{Matthew 23:36|23:36}}).
The words of Jesus are as reliable as the words of God (see {{Matthew 5:18|Matthew 5:18}}; {{Isaiah 40:8|Isaiah 40:8}}; {{Isaiah 55:11|55:11}}; {{Isaiah 59:21|59:21}}).

- *That day* is the day of judgment. 

- *nor the Son:* This phrase shows that Jesus did not know the exact time. {{Acts 1:7|Acts 1:7}} suggests the same idea. Because no one knows the day, Jesus told his followers to stay watchful and faithful (see {{Matthew 24:37-25:46|Matthew 24:37–25:46}}). This statement should discourage anyone from trying to calculate the exact date when our Lord will return.

- *at the coming of the Son of Man: *This refers to the second coming of Jesus (see {{Matthew 24:3|Matthew 24:3}}; compare {{Luke 17:26|Luke 17:26}}). 

- *in the days of Noah* (see {{Genesis 6:9-22|Genesis 6:9–22}}; {{2 Peter 2:5|2 Peter 2:5}}; {{2 Peter 3:5-6|3:5–6}}): This is not comparing how serious the sins were. Instead, it shows that people did not notice what God was doing. They were too focused on everyday pleasures and celebrations ({{Matthew 6:19-34|Matthew 6:19–34}}).

The second coming of Jesus will surprise people, just like the flood of Noah did ({{Genesis 7:1-24|Genesis 7}}). The only way to be ready is to live consistently alert and obedient (compare {{Luke 17:26-27|Luke 17:26–27}}, {{Luke 17:34-35|34–35}}).
Jesus now applied his prophecies ({{Matthew 24:1-36|Matthew 24:1–36}}) to his disciples so they would stay faithful and be ready for his second coming.

The word *taken* most likely means taken in judgment, either in AD 70 or at the end of history. *Left* would then mean remaining to enter a new time. This new time could be the age of the church (see {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}; {{Matthew 22:1-14|22:1–14}}) or the thousand–year reign of Christ on earth (the Millennium).
*keep watch:* This means to actively and energetically obey the Lord with a single focus (see {{Matthew 25:13|Matthew 25:13}}; {{Matthew 26:38-41|26:38–41}}).

*servant:* Those who were listening to Jesus might have thought of God's special servants, the prophets and lawgivers. But Jesus often used *servant* as a metaphor, so it is likely he was describing every disciple's responsibility (see {{Matthew 10:24-25|Matthew 10:24–25}}; {{Matthew 13:27-28|13:27–28}}; {{Matthew 18:23-35|18:23–35}}; {{Matthew 20:26|20:26}}).

This parable and the next three dramatize the importance of faithfully obeying while waiting for Jesus to return ({{Matthew 25:1-13|Matthew 25:1–13}}, {{Matthew 25:14-30|14–30}}, {{Matthew 25:31-46|31–46}}).

- *to meet the bridegroom: *This image points to the coming of the Messiah (see {{Mark 2:19-20|Mark 2:19–20}}). 

- We do not know the exact wedding customs of that time. Some believe the bridesmaids led the bride to the bridegroom's home. He stayed away until the wedding feast began. The bridesmaids would wait for his arrival and then escort him to the feast ({{Matthew 25:10|Matthew 25:10}}). 

Others think the bridegroom might have arrived late at night at the bride’s home, where they announced him. After celebrating with the bride’s guests, the groom would take his bride to his home under torches or lamps.

Jesus told a story about a wedding dinner. It was common for Jews to describe the coming of God’s kingdom as a feast. The wedding dinner in the parable was a feast to honour King Jesus.

In the story, five bridesmaids were ready when the groom came. Five weren’t ready when the groom arrived. The Messiah was urging his people to be ready for that important moment.
This parable confirms the need to be alert and ready for Christ's return ({{Matthew 25:13|Matthew 25:13}}; see also {{Luke 12:35-36|Luke 12:35–36}}).
Some people think the *oil *represents something specific (such as the Holy Spirit). But it more likely emphasizes the need to prepare for Christ's second coming.
Both the prudent and the foolish bridesmaids sleep while waiting. The parable criticizes only the foolish bridesmaids’ failure to bring enough oil.
The bridegroom arriving at midnight while the bridesmaids slept makes a further point: the second coming of Jesus will be sudden and unexpected ({{Matthew 24:42-51|Matthew 14:42–51}}).

God gives everyone gifts to use to serve him and others. He had given his people Israel the special gifts of his covenants and the Messiah.

Yet many of God’s people hadn’t been faithful to the covenants. And they didn’t accept Jesus as the Messiah.

Jesus told a story to show how dangerous this was for Israel. In the parable, two slaves used their gifts wisely. They were rewarded. The third slave did nothing with his gift. This slave is like those who refuse to trust God’s Son. This means they are choosing to not be a part of God’s family.

This parable teaches that the Lord expects his servants to be faithful to the task given to them while waiting for his return. The delay of Christ’s return will cause some to do evil things ({{Matthew 24:48-49|Matthew 24:48–49}}), some to become inactive ({{Matthew 25:3|25:3}}), and others may become fearfully passive ({{Matthew 25:18|25:18}}).
*After a long time:* This emphasizes the long wait for Christ's return ({{Matthew 24:45-51|Matthew 24:45–51}}).

- See {{Matthew 24:45-51|Matthew 24:45–51}}; {{Luke 16:10|Luke 16:10}}. 

- *Enter into the joy of your master!: *This shows the Father’s approval. It may also point to the Messiah’s great banquet (see {{Matthew 6:1|Matthew 6:1}}, {{Matthew 6:4|4}}, {{Matthew 6:6|6}}, {{Matthew 6:18|18}}; {{Matthew 9:9-17|9:9–17}}).
*I knew that you are a hard man:* This servant uses a false understanding of his master as an excuse for being lazy.
God gives plenty of grace to those who are faithful with what they already have (see {{Matthew 13:12|Matthew 13:12}}).
*sit on His glorious throne:* This represents a position of judgment (see {{Matthew 19:28|Matthew 19:28}}; {{Matthew 22:44|22:44}}; {{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}).

The last part of Jesus’ long message was about God’s family. It was also about Jesus bringing judgement. Only Jesus is wise enough to be the Judge of the whole world.

One day he will separate everything evil from everything good. He will judge all people for the way they treat his brothers and sisters. Those who follow Jesus are his brothers and sisters. They are joined together with Jesus very closely. They are so close that it’s like what happens to them also happens to Jesus. This is a wonderful mystery.

Jesus wants all people to follow his example of serving others. As they take care of others, they are serving Jesus.

This describes the final judgment of which Jesus had been warning (see {{Matthew 7:13-27|Matthew 7:13–27}}; {{Matthew 8:10-12|8:10–12}}; {{Matthew 11:20-24|11:20–24}}; {{Matthew 12:38-42|12:38–42}}; {{Matthew 13:24-30|13:24–30}}, {{Matthew 13:36-43|36–43}}; {{Matthew 16:24-28|16:24–28}}; {{Matthew 24:37-25:30|24:37–25:30}}).
*His right hand:* This is a place of honor ({{Genesis 48:13-20|Genesis 48:13–20}}; {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}).

*prepared for you from the foundation of the world:* This phrase might be a reference to God choosing people for salvation before time began (see {{Matthew 13:10-17|Matthew 13:10–17}}; {{Ephesians 1:4|Ephesians 1:4}}; {{Revelation 17:8|Revelation 17:8}}). Or it might only refer to the God's kingdom as a place (compare {{Matthew 25:41|Matthew 25:41}}).

The actions mentioned here are often called "deeds of mercy." These were acts of kindness toward those in need (see {{Isaiah 58:1-12|Isaiah 58:1–12}}; {{Ezekiel 18:7|Ezekiel 18:7}}; {{James 1:26-27|James 1:26–27}}). These good deeds are not efforts to earn God's approval. Instead, they come from a love for Christ that results in compassion toward others (see {{Matthew 6:1-4|Matthew 6:1–4}}).

These *righteous* people (see {{Matthew 5:6|Mathhew 5:6}}, {{Matthew 5:20|20}}) obey God's will as Jesus taught them. They show this most clearly through acts of love ({{Matthew 7:12|7:12}}; {{Matthew 9:9-13|9:9–13}}; {{Matthew 22:34-40|22:34–40}}; {{Matthew 25:35-40|25:35–40}}).

*these brothers of Mine:* This phrase may show the close bond Jesus had with his disciples (see {{Matthew 10:42|10:42}}; {{Matthew 18:1-14|18:1–14}}; {{Galatians 6:10|Galatians 6:10}}). Or it could refer to all humanity, regardless of their faith (see {{Matthew 6:1-4|Matthew 6:1–4}}; {{Matthew 25:43|25:43}}; {{Proverbs 19:17|Proverbs 19:17}}). The phrase *brothers of Mine* suggests the first meaning ({{Matthew 12:46-50|Matthew 12:46–50}}; {{Matthew 18:15-35|18:15–35}}; {{Matthew 23:8|23:8}}; {{Matthew 28:10|28:10}}). But it does not exclude the duty to care for others in general (see {{Luke 10:30-37|Luke 10:30–37}}).

The Greek word for *eternal* can mean "lasting forever" or "lasting for an age." It refers to "the age to come" ({{Matthew 13:39-40|Matthew 13:39–40}}, {{Matthew 13:49|49}}; {{Matthew 24:3|24:3}}; {{John 17:3|John 17:3}}; {{2 Thessalonians 1:9|2 Thessalonians 1:9}}; {{Philemon 15|Philemon 1:15}}; {{1 John 5:11|1 John 5:11}}, {{1 John 5:13|13}}). 

Some hope that the punishment of the damned will end after "an age." God will either destroy or forgive them. Yet, the comparison between *eternal life* and *eternal punishment* strongly suggests it means "lasting forever." This is because *eternal life* does not end (see also {{Luke 16:19-31|Luke 16:19–31}}; {{Hebrews 6:2|Hebrews 6:2}}; {{Revelation 20:10|Revelation 20:10}}).

Jesus knew that one of his disciples would turn against him. He knew that Israel’s leaders would use violence against him.

When the woman poured perfume on Jesus’ head the disciples thought it was a waste. It made the disciples angry. But Jesus knew it wasn’t a waste. The woman was helping Jesus prepare to be buried.

This sounded like very bad news. But Jesus knew it would lead to good news that would spread everywhere on earth.

The irony is that the Son of Man, who will one day judge the nations ({{Matthew 25:31-46|Matthew 25:31–46}}), must first be unfairly judged and condemned to death by evil people. The death of Jesus was the ultimate Passover sacrifice (see {{John 19:31-37|John 19:31–37}}; {{1 Corinthians 5:7|1 Corinthians 5:7}}).

- *Caiaphas* was the high priest. He lived near the temple in Jerusalem's upper city. This meeting was not at the usual place or time, so it was urgent and probably secret. The Sanhedrin (the official Jewish council) usually met in the council chamber. The council chamber was located either at the southern end of the court of the Israelites in the temple or on the western edge of the temple hill. 

- Joseph Caiaphas was the son-in-law of Annas (see {{John 18:13|John 18:13}}). He served as high priest from AD 18 to 36 ({{John 11:49|John 11:49}}). He had the longest term of any high priest from Herod's rule until AD 70. They had removed Annas, his father-in-law, from his position but he was still called high priest as well (see {{Luke 3:2|Luke 3:2}}; {{John 18:13|John 18:13}}, {{John 18:19-24|19–24}}).

At Passover, Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. The Jewish leaders feared losing their authority if they caused or permitted anything that looked like a revolt against Rome (see {{Matthew 21:8-11|Matthew 21:8–11}}, {{Matthew 21:14-16|14–16}}).

Simon was a man who had once suffered from leprosy. Jesus being in his home showed the forgiving and healing love that Jesus often gave to people who were outcasts (see {{Matthew 8:7|8:7}}; {{Matthew 9:10|9:10}}).

A similar anointing happened earlier in Galilee ({{Luke 7:36-50|Luke 7:36–50}}). Matthew includes this event here (compare {{John 12:1-8|John 12:1–8}}) to highlight different responses to Jesus. While the Jewish leaders were plotting to kill Jesus ({{Matthew 26:3-5|Matthew 26:3–5}}) and Judas was preparing to betray him ({{Matthew 26:14-16|26:14–16}}), the woman honored Jesus with her actions.

The jar of costly perfume was used for burial customs (see {{Mark 16:1|Mark 16:1}}; {{Luke 23:56-24:1|Luke 23:56–24:1}}; {{John 12:1-7|John 12:1–7}}; {{John 19:38-42|19:38–42}}). It was made from nard, a plant harvested in India. The perfume was worth almost a full year’s wages({{John 12:5|John 12:5}}).
*they were indignant:* {{John 12:4|John 12:4}} shows that Judas Iscariot caused this reaction.

*prepared My body for burial:* We do not know if the woman fully understood what she was doing. The anointing also symbolizes Jesus as king and priest ({{1 Samuel 10:1|1 Samuel 10:1}}; {{2 Kings 9:6|2 Kings 9:6}}; {{Exodus 29:7|Exodus 29:7}}).

Judas sold himself to the authorities (see also {{John 11:57|John 11:57}}), kept it secret ({{Matthew 26:25|Matthew 26:25}}), and led them to Jesus at the right time to arrest him ({{Matthew 26:47-56|26:47–56}}; see {{John 18:2|John 18:2}}). Later, feeling guilty, Judas killed himself ({{Matthew 27:3-10|Matthew 27:3–10}}; see {{Acts 1:15-22|Acts 1:15–22}}). 

Judas was known for his greed ({{Matthew 26:14-15|Matthew 26:14–15}}; {{John 12:4-6|John 12:4–6}}; {{John 13:29|13:29}}). Some think he may also have been disappointed in the kind of Messiah Jesus was, ashamed after the anointing of Jesus (see {{John 12:1-8|John 12:1–8}}). Others think he may have been resentful of the leadership of Peter, James, and John. Whatever his reasons, Judas’s betrayal was still part of God’s larger plan ({{Acts 1:16-17|Acts 1:16–17}}).

The Passover Feast was a powerful reminder of God’s covenant with his people Israel in the Old Testament.

God was about to establish a new covenant through the death and resurrection of Jesus. The new covenant is for all people who believe in Jesus.

Jesus was showing his disciples the purpose for his death. His death would set people free from the power of sin, death and evil. Jesus used bread and wine as signs to teach about this new freedom. He would give up his body like the bread he served the disciples at dinner. Like the wine he poured, blood would flow out of him as he was killed. This is how he would accomplish the work God sent him to do.
*My time:* The Messiah would now complete the work for which he was commissioned, to die for the sins of the world.

*dipped his hand into the bowl with Me:* Everyone would dip their food into a shared bowl, which probably had herbs and fruit puree in it. Sharing a meal showed friendship and trust, so having a betrayer there was shocking ({{Matthew 26:21|Matthew 26:21}}; but see {{John 13:26|John 13:26}}).

*as it is written:* Jesus might have been referring to {{Isaiah 53:7-9|Isaiah 53:7–9}} or the broader Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. This verse shows both God's sovereign will and human responsibility.

- Judas referred to Jesus as *Rabbi*, but the other disciples call him "Lord" ({{Matthew 26:22|Mathhew 26:22}}). 

- *You have said it yourself:* This mysterious statement confirmed that Judas was the betrayer.

- {{Deuteronomy 16:3|Deuteronomy 16:3}}calls the unleavened bread of the Passover (see {{Exodus 12:18|Exodus 12:18}}) the "bread of affliction." This is because it symbolizes the hardships in Egypt. 

- During the Passover meal, the traditional blessing over the bread is: "Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who brings forth bread from the earth."

- *gave thanks:* The traditional blessing for the Passover cup was “Blessed are you, O Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates the fruit of the vine.” An early Christian version is “We give thanks to you, our Father, for the Holy Vine of David, your child, whom you revealed to us through Jesus your child; glory be to you forever” (*Didache* 9.2). 

- The four cups of the Passover meal match the four promises in {{Exodus 6:6-7|Exodus 6:6–7}}: two for deliverance, one for redemption (see {{Matthew 26:27-28|Matthew 26:27–28}}), and one for fellowship (see {{Matthew 26:29|26:29}}).

- *the covenant:* In God’s covenant with Israel, the blood of sheep or goats was shed and put on the doorposts at Passover ({{Exodus 12:5|Exodus 12:5}}, {{Exodus 12:13|13}}; {{Exodus 24:8|24:8}}). They put it on the "the sides and tops of the doorframes" ({{Exodus 12:7|Exodus 12:7}}). Jesus, the sinless Lamb of God, created a new *covenant *with his blood (see {{Jeremiah 31:31|Jeremiah 31:31}}). The *covenant* represents God's self-initiated promise to bring salvation to humanity, fulfilling the promise to the patriarch Abraham (see {{Genesis 12:1-20|Genesis 12}}; {{Galatians 3:15-29|Galatians 3:15–29}}; {{Galatians 4:12-31|4:12–31}}). 

- *for many for the forgiveness of sins:* Jesus shed his blood as a sacrifice to forgive *sins* (see {{Jeremiah 31:31-34|Jeremiah 31:31–34}}; {{Mark 14:24|Mark 14:24}}). Some think *many* means only God's chosen people, while others believe it means "all" (compare {{Matthew 20:28|Matthew 20:28}}).

- *until that day:* The kingdom of God began with the ministry of Jesus, but it is not yet complete. It still awaits its full completion at the end (see {{1 Corinthians 15:20-28|1 Corinthians 15:20–28}}; {{Revelation 19:1-22:21|Revelation 19–22}}). 

- *until that day when I drink it anew:* Jesus describes the final completion of the kingdom as a great feast, like the Passover. This picture shows eternal fellowship with God and his people, marked by love and peace.
*when they had sung a hymn:* Some people think they sang the *Great Hallel *({{Psalm 136:1-26|Psalm 136}}).

*I will strike:* In {{Zechariah 13:7-9|Zechariah 13:7–9}}, a sword strikes God's partner, the Shepherd. Jesus understood this as a prophecy of his own death. From the scattered sheep, a purified group of faithful ones will emerge ({{Zechariah 13:8-9|Zechariah 13:8–9}}). In the short term, the disciples would soon scatter and deny knowing Jesus ({{Matthew 26:34|Matthew 26:34}}, {{Matthew 26:56|56}}, {{Matthew 26:69-75|69–75}}).

Jesus was deeply sad and troubled. He was about to do the hardest part of his work to free God’s people. He would have to face his hardest battle against evil without his disciples. They would all run away.

With painful honesty he turned to his Father in prayer. He had hoped his disciples would pray with him, but they fell asleep. His Father had given him strength throughout the time that he had been working on earth. Jesus prayed that what God wanted to happen would be done on earth.
Jesus prophesied a time when the disciples would return, even though they were about to leave him (see chapter {{Matthew 28:1-20|Matthew 28}}; {{John 21:1-25|John 21}}).
Peter’s denial is the most well-known. But all the other disciples also left Jesus or avoided being connected with him (see {{Matthew 26:56|26:56}}).

*Gethsemane* is an olive orchard about 229 meters (about 250 yards) east of Jerusalem's Golden Gate. It is above the Kidron Valley on the Mount of Olives. Jesus and his disciples often met there ({{Luke 22:39-40|Luke 22:39–40}}; {{John 18:1-2|John 18:1–2}}).

This scene reveals how deeply Jesus understood the suffering he would encounter on the cross. It also reveals his complete dedication to God's will (see {{Matthew 20:28|Matthew 20:28}}). The words in {{Matthew 26:41-42|26:41–42}} echo the Lord’s Prayer in {{Matthew 6:9-13|6:9–13}}.

- *He took with Him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee:* Peter, James, and John were probably the leaders of the apostles. They received special revelation (Peter, James, and John were present at the Transfiguration, where they saw Jesus transformed on the mountain, {{Matthew 17:1-13|Matthew 17:1–13}}). They stayed with Jesus during this difficult time. 

- Jesus felt *sorrow* and *distress* as he thought about the Father’s plan for him (see {{Matthew 27:45-46|Matthew 27:45–46}}). Though he had never sinned, Jesus would take on humanity’s sin so that people could become "the righteousness of God" in Jesus ({{2 Corinthians 5:21|2 Corinthians 5:21}}).

- *if it is possible:* Jesus desired to obey the Father fully while dreading the suffering and judgment he was about to bear.

- *Yet not as I will, but as You will:* He continued to do the Father's will ({{Matthew 4:1-11|Matthew 4:1–11}}; {{Matthew 16:23|16:23}}; {{John 6:38|John 6:38}}).

Jesus’ disciple Judas Iscariot turned against him. Judas handed Jesus over to people who wanted to harm him.

One of Jesus’ disciples tried to defend him with a sword. But Jesus healed the person who was hurt. Jesus remained calm and refused to use violence against human beings.

He explained that he could have stopped what was happening. But instead he allowed himself to be arrested. Jesus was committed to obeying God and doing the work God gave him to do. His work wasn’t to fight humans but to save them from evil.
*kissed Him:* Judas used a sign of friendship to betray Jesus. This makes his betrayal even worse.
*one of Jesus’ companions:* This was Peter ({{John 18:26|John 18:26}}).
*twelve legions:* Jesus used Roman military language to describe the help he could receive from God. A legion was about 6,000 soldiers. Jesus was not a helpless victim. He allowed his own arrest.
If Jesus had resisted, it would have blocked the fulfillment of God’s saving work (see {{Matthew 16:21-23|Matthew 16:21–23}}).
The leaders acted secretly because they feared the people who honored Jesus (see {{Matthew 21:26|Matthew 21:26}}, {{Matthew 21:46|46}}; {{Matthew 26:3-5|26:3–5}}).

- We do not know which of the Scriptures Jesus was referring to. It might have been {{Isaiah 53:1-12|Isaiah 53}} or the general Old Testament theme of a suffering Messiah. 

- As Jesus had predicted earlier that evening, all the disciples adandoned him ({{Matthew 26:31-35|Matthew 26:31–35}}).

The Roman government didn’t allow Jewish religious leaders to put people to death. So the Jewish leaders wanted the Romans to put Jesus to death.

They hoped to get Jesus in trouble for claiming to be the messiah. It was thought that the messiah would be a rebel warrior who fought against the government. That charge would make the Romans put Jesus to death.

Jesus didn’t argue with the leaders or say that he wasn’t the Messiah. Instead, Jesus talked about himself again as the Son of Man.

The Sanhedrin claimed that he was saying evil things that led people away from God. This was a crime worthy of death according to the Law of Moses (Deuteronomy 13:1–5).

This hearing was probably an informal meeting to agree on the charges. The Jewish leaders faced pressure to keep the hearing secret to avoid a riot (see {{Matthew 21:26|Matthew 21:26}}, {{Matthew 21:46|46}}; {{Matthew 26:5|26:5}}, {{Matthew 26:55|55}}; {{John 11:45-53|John 11:45–53}}).
*the courtyard of the high priest:* This place indicates an unplanned meeting of the Sanhedrin at the high priest's palace ({{Matthew 26:3|Matthew 26:3}}).
*were seeking false testimony:* The verb tense suggests a long and possibly desperate attempt to find any testimony to support a formal accusation (see {{Mark 14:55-56|Mark 14:55–56}}).

*they did not find any:* This was because the evidence was too weak or inconsistent to seek a death sentence. This changed when two men gave testimonies that matched ({{Deuteronomy 17:6|Deuteronomy 17:6}}; {{Deuteronomy 19:15|19:15}}).
The charge was either a misunderstanding or a deliberate misrepresentation of what Jesus had said about his death and resurrection (see {{John 2:19-21|John 2:19–21}}).
*if You are the Christ:* The high priest asked this because {{Zechariah 6:12|Zechariah 6:12}} prophesied that the Christ (Messiah) would rebuild the temple (compare {{Matthew 26:61|Matthew 26:61}}).

- *You have said it yourself:* This was a careful but clear “yes” (see {{Matthew 26:25|Matthew 26:25}}; {{Matthew 27:11|27:11}}). In Mark’s account Jesus answers, “I Am” ({{Mark 14:62|Mark 14:62}}). 

- *you will see:* By quoting {{Daniel 7:13|Daniel 7:13}}, Jesus confirmed he was the Son of Man who God would vindicate and honor.

- *sitting at the right hand of Power:* See {{Psalm 110:1|Psalm 110:1}}. Jews often avoided saying God's name directly (see study note on Matthew 5:4). 

- The phrase *coming on the clouds of heaven* might refer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70 or to the return of Jesus at the end of history.

*He has blasphemed: *Caiaphas thought Jesus had spoken against God (blasphemed) when Jesus claimed to be the Son of Man. The title "Son of Man" was very special. It described someone who shared God's glory and power ({{Daniel 7:13-14|Daniel 7:13–14}}).

This abuse fulfills the prophecies in {{Isaiah 50:6|Isaiah 50:6}} and {{Isaiah 53:4-9|53:4–9}}. Jesus himself prophesied these things ({{Matthew 16:21|Matthew 16:21}}; {{Matthew 17:22-23|17:22–23}}; {{Matthew 20:18-19|20:18–19}}; {{Matthew 26:2|26:2}}; see also {{Mark 14:65|Mark 14:65}}).

Peter had boldly promised to always be faithful to Jesus (Matthew 26:35). But when he found himself in danger, he broke his promise.

Three times he said he didn’t know Jesus. Peter was filled with terrible sadness when he realised what he had done.

Jesus knew Peter and he knew Peter’s weaknesses. But Jesus still loved Peter.

Later he would welcome Peter back into the community of disciples.
Peter's denials fulfill what Jesus prophesied ({{Matthew 26:34|Matthew 26:34}}).
*your accent:* Jews from Galilee spoke with a distinct accent compared to those from Judea (see {{Matthew 4:13|Matthew 4:13}} and the related study note).
The crow of the rooster reminded Peter of what Jesus predicted would happen ({{Matthew 26:34|26:34}}). Peter felt deep sorrow.

The Jewish leaders said Jesus had spoken blasphemy ({{Matthew 26:65-66|26:65–66}}). That charge was enough for the death penalty under Jewish law, but it would not persuade a Roman judge. So the leading priests and elders worked together to create a political charge that would fit Roman law on capital offenses (see {{Matthew 27:11-26|27:11–26}}; {{Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2}}).
The Jewish leaders prepared charges against Jesus so that Pilate would order his death. Pilate, a Gentile, fulfills the prediction of Jesus from {{Matthew 20:19|Matthew 20:19}}.

Peter lied about knowing Jesus, and Judas turned Jesus over to his enemies. Jesus later forgave Peter and helped him to be one of the disciples again. This was different from what happened with Judas.

Judas had received money for turning against Jesus. Long ago the prophets Zechariah and Jeremiah had talked about those silver coins.

After he handed Jesus over, Judas didn’t want the money anymore. He realised that he had helped put someone to death who wasn’t guilty. He felt very sad and was sorry about what he had done. But he didn’t allow himself to be forgiven or brought back into the community. Instead, Judas hung himself.

Tiberius Caesar made Pilate the governor (or prefect) of Judea. Pilate mainly governed from Caesarea, not Jerusalem, from AD 26 to AD 36. Although he had full power in Judea, Pilate answered to the governor (or legate) of Syria. This man was the main authority in the eastern Roman Empire. The Jewish historian Josephus records several mentions of Pilate. Pilate's disrespect for the holiness of Jewish customs caused revolts.

Judas felt deep remorse (the Greek word *metamelomai*), but he did not repent (the Greek word *metanoeō*). Repentance would have changed his heart and led to obedience and a relationship with God through faith.

There are two stories about Judas's death. This one and the one found in {{Acts 1:18-19|Acts 1:18–19}}. There are differences between the two stories:

- Matthew says the priests bought the field ({{Matthew 27:6-7|Matthew 27:6–7}}), but Acts suggests Judas bought it ({{Acts 1:18|Acts 1:18}}). 

- Matthew says Judas hanged himself by hanging ({{Matthew 27:5|Matthew 27:5}}). Acts says he fell and his body burst open ({{Acts 1:18|Acts 1:18}}).

- Matthew says the field of blood was named for its use as a burial place ({{Matthew 27:7-8|Matthew 27:7–8}}). Acts says it was named because of Judas’s violent death ({{Acts 1:19|Acts 1:19}}). 

The stories can align if Acts describes the results of Matthew's events.

*innocent blood: *The innocence of Jesus is a key theme in the story of his suffering (see {{Matthew 23:35|Matthew 23:35}}; {{Matthew 26:55-56|26:55–56}}, {{Matthew 26:59-60|59–60}}; {{Matthew 27:18-19|27:18–19}}, {{Matthew 27:24|24}}; see also {{Luke 23:47|Luke 23:47}}).

*hanged himself: *Judas killed himself because he felt guilty but did not repent. His death also matched the Old Testament law about punishing a false witness (see {{Deuteronomy 19:16-21|Deuteronomy 19:16–21}}).

*foreigners:* These were non-Jewish people who died in Jerusalem. If they could not find the owner of donated money, they used it for public charity. In this case, they used money considered ceremonially unclean to buy a ceremonially unclean place for people considered ceremonially unclean.
*Field of Blood:* This is another way of describing a cemetery (compare {{Acts 1:18-19|Acts 1:18–19}}).

- *what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet was fulfilled:* The quote is from {{Zechariah 11:12-13|Zechariah 11:12–13}}. Matthew might have followed the Jewish tradition of naming books by the first book in the scroll. In this case, Jeremiah would be the first book in the scroll containing Zechariah. Or, Matthew might be referencing similar passages in Jeremiah ({{Jeremiah 19:1-13|Jeremiah 19:1–13}}; {{Jeremiah 18:2-6|18:2–6}}; {{Jeremiah 32:6-15|32:6–15}}) along with {{Zechariah 11:12-13|Zechariah 11:12–13}}. 

- Matthew notices a strong similarity between Zechariah's actions and those of the leading priests. Both situations involve rejecting God's messenger, who was meant to be the king of God's people.

*King of the Jews:* The Sanhedrin's first charge of blasphemy in {{Matthew 26:65-66|Matthew 26:65–66}}; {{Matthew 27:1|27:1}} did not cause concern for the Romans. The Romabs considered it to be a Jewish religious issue (see {{Acts 25:18-20|Acts 25:18–20}}). So, the Sanhedrin changed the charge to make Jesus seem like a political rebel to the Romans (see {{Luke 23:2|Luke 23:2}}).

Pilate was the Roman governor of Judea. During Jesus’ trial, Pilate wanted to know if Jesus was a king. Would Jesus lead the Jewish people to attack the Roman government?

Pilate quickly understood that Jesus wasn’t dangerous or violent. But Pilate had to stay in control of the crowd and avoid a fight during Passover. So Pilate did what he knew was wrong. He sentenced Jesus to be nailed to a cross. Pilate did this even though Jesus wasn’t guilty of anything.

Pilate washed his hands as a sign that he wasn’t guilty of Jesus’ death. Yet the water couldn’t wash away his guilt. The Jewish leaders were guilty. The shouting crowd was also guilty. Jesus would die because of the wrong things that others had done.

The Roman trial included an initial hearing before Pilatee ({{Matthew 27:11-14|Matthew 27:11–14}}), then one before Herod Antipas ({{Luke 23:6-16|Luke 23:6–16}}), and a second hearing with Pilate ({{Matthew 27:15-26|Matthew 27:15–26}}).

Pilate's behavior seems unusual. It was not normal for him to try to please his Jewish subjects. But Pilate's relationship with Caesar might have been unstable at this time (see study note on John 19:12; see Philo, *On the Embassy to Gaius* 159–161). If so, this gesture might have been to maintain peace and avoid negative attention from Rome.

*notorious prisoner named Barabbas:* He is also called an "insurrectionist" ({{Mark 15:7|Mark 15:7}}; {{John 18:40|John 18:40}}). This word can also mean a robber or someone who led a revolt (see {{Luke 23:19|Luke 23:19}}). To the zealots, Barabbas was considered a hero.
*have suffered terribly in a dream* (compare {{Matthew 1:20|Matthew 1:20}}): It is notable that a pagan woman recognized Jesus innocence and spoke up for him, while the Jewish crowd did not.
*You bear the responsibility:* The priests told Judas the same thing ({{Matthew 27:4|Matthew 27:4}}).

- *All the people* (see {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}): This does not mean every living Jewish person. Instead, it refers to those who urged the condemnation of Jesus. They represented all of Israel who disbelieved Jesus. Their actions led to consequences for the entire nation, like the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70. 

- *His blood be on us and on our children!* (see {{Matthew 23:35|23:35}}; {{2 Samuel 1:16|2 Samuel 1:16}}; {{2 Samuel 14:9|14:9}}; {{Jeremiah 51:35|Jeremiah 51:35}}; {{Acts 5:28|Acts 5:28}}; {{Acts 18:6|18:6}}; {{Acts 20:26|20:26}}): Some Christians have misunderstood and misused this verse as a basis for persecuting Jews. But it is not a general accusation against all Jewish people.

When the Romans flogged a man, they beat him with whips that had leather straps on the end. Some straps had sharp bone, lead, or rock pieces attached (see also {{Deuteronomy 25:1-3|Deuteronomy 25:1–3}}; {{1 Kings 12:11|1 Kings 12:11}}, {{1 Kings 12:14|14}}; {{Acts 16:22|Acts 16:22}}; {{Acts 22:25|22:25}}; {{2 Corinthians 11:24-25|2 Corinthians 11:24–25}}).

- *the governor's soldiers* were extra troops recruited from non-Jewish residents of Palestine. 

- The soldiers stayed at the governor's official building in Jerusalem. This building was called the Antonia Fortress. It stood at the northwest corner of the Temple area.
During the Jewish trial, people mocked Jesus as a prophet ({{Matthew 26:67-68|Matthew 26:67–68}}). Here, they mocked him as a king.

Many people made fun of Jesus as he was dying. The Roman soldiers made mean jokes about Jesus being a king. People passing by mocked him for not being able to save himself from death.

Israel’s leaders and the criminals hanging beside Jesus also made fun of him. They thought that a real messiah would save the people and himself. They thought that a real king wouldn’t be killed on the cross.

Yet the crown of thorns and the sign above Jesus’ head showed things that were true. He was Israel’s King. And it was by dying that he would bring salvation to God’s people.

- The *scarlet robe* was probably a soldier's cloak used to imitate royal clothing in order to mock Jesus. 

- Weaving *a crown of thorns* was meant to mock Jesus as a king.

Usually, the person to be crucified would carry their own cross. They only carried the crossbeam since the vertical pole was already at the crucifixion site. The Romans might have forced Simon to help because Jesus was weak from being whipped. Making Simon help could also have been a way to mock Jesus. They treated him like someone who deserved a servant, even though they led him to his death.
The crowd mocked Jesus, but their words were still true. He is the Son of God, the King of Israel, and the Messiah.

- They probably gave Jesus wine mixed with bitter gall to ridicule him (see {{Psalm 69:21|Psalm 69:21}}). It also was a sedative. Jesus probably refused it so he could fully experience suffering for our sins (see {{Isaiah 53:10|Isaiah 53:10}}). 

- *Gall* is another name sometimes given to wormwood. It is a very bitter substance made from the oil of the *Artemisia* plant, sometimes used as medicine in the ancient world (compare {{Mark 15:23|Mark 15:23}}).

*they had crucified Him:* Crucifixion (being nailed to a cross) was not common among Jews. But it was a widespread Roman punishment for military and political offenders. This was especially true for slaves, rebels, and insurrectionists (rioters). The extreme cruelty and public display of crucifixion was a strong warning to society. 

The Romans would flog victims (beat them with whips). Then they would crucify the victims naked. This added to their humiliation. Most considered it the most painful death possible. It involved intense suffering, exposure to weather and insects, and suffocation. It often concluded with a final violent spear thrust to end life. 

Since the Law said that anyone hung on a tree was under God’s curse ({{Deuteronomy 21:22-23|Deuteronomy 21:22–23}}), crucifixion was especially offensive to the Jewish people. Yet in God’s plan, what humans saw as shameful became the very means of salvation. Earlier, Jesus had told his disciples to take up their cross and follow him ({{Matthew 16:24|Matthew 16:24}}).
The Romans would fasten the official crime to the cross above the head of the offender. They accused Jesus of political rebellion.
Jesus was crucified between two convicted revolutionaries. This increased his shame and made him appear guilty by association (linked with rebels).

*If You are the Son of God:* This taunt reminds us of when the devil tempted Jesus at the start of his public ministry ({{Matthew 4:1-11|Matthew 4:1–11}}). The devil tried to use the special status of Jesus to tempt him to avoid suffering (see also {{Matthew 16:21-23|16:21–23}}).

*darkness:* This represents God's judgment. Or, it could more specifically refer to the coming of the day of the Lord (see {{Amos 5:18|Amos 5:18}}, {{Amos 5:20|20}}; {{Amos 8:9-10|8:9–10}}; also {{Jeremiah 4:27-28|Jeremiah 4:27–28}}; {{Jeremiah 13:16|13:16}}; {{Jeremiah 15:9|15:9}}).

When Jesus died, he broke the control that sin and death had over God’s world. As a sign of this the earth shook, split and broke open. Tombs opened up and some people were raised from the dead. It was the beginning of something completely new.

But Jesus’ body had no more life in it. His body was taken down from the cross. Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy leader in the Jewish Council. He took care of Jesus’ body after he died and put it in his own tomb. The tomb was secured by guards and a big stone.

- *Eli, Eli:* This cry means *My God, My God.* The sound of these words may have made some people think Jesus was calling for Elijah ({{Matthew 27:47|Matthew 27:47}}). 

- *My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?:* Jesus was expressing the weight of judgment he bore for humanity’s sin.
Many Jews believed Elijah would return before the day of the Lord ({{Matthew 11:14-15|Matthew 11:14–15}}; {{Matthew 17:10-13|17:10–13}}; {{Malachi 4:5|Malachi 4:5}}).
