The *sour wine* was vinegar. The drink was probably meant to mock Jesus by pretending to ease his thirst (compare {{Psalm 69:21|Psalm 69:21}} with {{Matthew 27:34|Matthew 27:34}}). Although some scholars think they offered it as a genuine act of kindness.

- Each of the four gospels focuses on different parts of the final moments of Jesus. 

- *He yielded up His spirit:* Jesus gave up his life willingly. This shows his authority, since he chose the moment of his own death (see also {{John 19:30|John 19:30}}). 

- *Jesus had cried out again* (see {{Matthew 27:46|Matthew 27:46}}): This final loud cry was the last prayer of Jesus (see {{Luke 23:46|Luke 23:46}}).

- The tearing of the temple curtain is symbolic. It means that that the wall dividing people from God has been torn down by the death of Jesus (see also {{Ephesians 2:11-22|Ephesians 2:11–22}}; {{Hebrews 6:19|Hebrews 6:19}}; {{Hebrews 9:1-10:25|9:1–10:25}}). 

- *The earth quaked and the rocks were split:* These are signs that judgment has come (see {{Exodus 19:18|Exodus 19:18}}; {{Judges 5:4|Judges 5:4}}; {{Psalm 18:7|Psalm 18:7}}; {{Joel 3:14-17|Joel 3:14–17}}; {{Amos 8:8-10|Amos 8:8–10}}). The Jewish historian Josephus records that around AD 30, a star resembling a sword appeared and the temple gates opened by themselves (Josephus, *War* 6.5.3–4).

- *The tombs broke open:* At the moment of the death of Jesus, God’s kingdom broke into the world in a new way. His death destroyed the power of death and began the promise of final resurrection (see {{Isaiah 26:19|Isaiah 26:19}}; {{Daniel 12:2|Daniel 12:2}}; {{1 Corinthians 15:1-58|1 Corinthians 15:1–58}}; {{Colossians 1:18|Colossians 1:18}}; {{Hebrews 2:14-15|Hebrews 2:14–15}}). 

- Some holy people were raised to life. But they may not have entered Jerusalem until after Jesus rose from the dead. Another view is that they were not raised until after the resurrection of Jesus, since Jesus is the “firstfruits” (the first to be raised, showing what will come for others; see {{1 Corinthians 15:20|1 Corinthians 15:20}}, {{1 Corinthians 15:23|23}}; {{Colossians 1:18|Colossians 1:18}}). If this second view is correct, Matthew included the story to show the great impact of the death of Jesus.

- The Roman officer and the other soldiers were not Jewish. 

- *the Son of God: *This could be a clear statement that Jesus is the unique Son of God (see {{Matthew 14:33|Matthew 14:33}}; {{Matthew 16:16|16:16}}) or perhaps a general statement about the innocence of Jesus (see {{Luke 23:47|Luke 23:47}}). They reacted to the earthquake and everything that happened as signs of divine involvement in this event.

- In Roman crucifixion, the bodies of criminals were often left on the cross until they rotted. Jewish law, however, did not allow this. {{Deuteronomy 21:22-23|Deuteronomy 21:22–23}} forbids leaving a body on a cross or gallows overnight. Joseph of Arimathea acted in line with this law when he asked for the body of Jesus. His request also showed his loyalty to Jesus.

- *Pilate ordered:* Pilate agreed to Joseph’s request and gave the order. He likely did this because he did not believe Jesus was guilty of rebellion against Rome (see {{Matthew 27:24-26|Matthew 27:24–26}}).

- Burial customs were important in Judaism, unlike the Greeks and Romans who cremated their dead. Jews considered leaving a body unburied to be a severe punishment ({{Deuteronomy 21:22-23|Deuteronomy 21:22–23}}; {{2 Kings 9:37|2 Kings 9:37}}; {{Psalm 79:3|Psalm 79:3}}; {{Jeremiah 16:4|Jeremiah 16:4}}, {{Jeremiah 16:6|6}}; {{Ezekiel 29:5|Ezekiel 29:5}}; {{Revelation 11:9|Revelation 11:9}}). 

People mourned and lamented death ({{Mark 5:38-39|Mark 5:38–39}}). They washed the body ({{Acts 9:37|Acts 9:37}}). They anointed the body ({{Matthew 26:6-13|Matt 26:6–13}}; {{John 12:3|John 12:3}}, {{John 12:7|7}}; {{John 19:39|19:39}}). And they wrapped the body in burial cloths ({{Matthew 27:59|Matthew 27:59}}; see {{Genesis 50:2-3|Genesis 50:2–3}}). Then they placed the body in a tomb ({{Matthew 23:27|Matthew 23:27}}). This tomb was either tunneled into rock or carved into a cave wall. A large stone often sealed the tomb to prevent ceremonial uncleanness or stealing. 

- *clean linen … new tomb: *These terms symbolize ceremonial purity. Joseph of Arimathea bought the tomb for his family, but had not used it.
This event supports the truth of Jesus resurrection. It is very unlikely that Matthew invented the story, because many witnesses were alive who could have denied it.

*Mary Magdalene *(see {{Matthew 27:56|Matthew 27:56}}): Mentioning two women as witnesses adds credibility to the story. In those times, people considered the testimony of a woman less reliable than a man. So a someone making up a false story would not have chosen women as witnesses.

The four gospels each emphasize different aspects of the empty tomb and resurrection appearances. Matthew focuses on three things: 

- the reunion of Jesus and his disciples in Galilee, 

- the Jewish leaders' attempt to discredit the resurrection, and 

- the importance of the ressurection for the salvation of the world.

Mary Magdalene and another woman named Mary went to the tomb to honour Jesus.

An angel told them Jesus wasn’t there because he had risen from the dead. The women became the first witnesses of Jesus’ resurrection.

Jesus had won the battle over death! He was raised to new life. Sin and death were God’s enemies. God won the victory over them through Jesus’ death.

The women were afraid but also filled with joy. When they met Jesus, they worshipped him at once.

The religious leaders paid the guards to lie about what had happened. Jesus had said many times that he would rise from the dead. The leaders didn’t want anyone to believe that Jesus had been telling the truth.

- Such a bribe was against the law (see {{Exodus 20:16|Exodus 20:16}}; {{Exodus 23:8|23:8}}). 

- *elders:* See the study note on Matthew 21:23.
*stole him away:* Stealing from tombs was common in ancient times. So this accusation would have been easy to believe.

*And this account has been circulated among the Jews to this very day: *Around AD 165, the early church father Justin Martyr wrote to the Jews of his time. He wrote, “You have sent . . . men throughout all the world to proclaim, ‘A godless and lawless heresy has sprung from one Jesus, a Galilean deceiver, whom we crucified, but his disciples stole him by night from the tomb . . . and now [the disciples] deceive men by asserting that he has risen from the dead and ascended into heaven’” (Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho* 108). 

This false information probably increased after the disciples began preaching about the resurrection of Jesus (see {{Acts 2:22-36|Acts 2:22–36}}).

The disciples saw Jesus and worshipped him on a mountain in Galilee. His final words were about his authority and how the disciples must continue his work.

Jesus has authority over the whole world. He brought God’s rule to earth. Jesus told his disciples to keep doing the work that he did on earth. They must invite people everywhere to be part of God’s family. The victory of Jesus the Messiah must be announced to all nations.

Jesus is the King for all people to worship and obey. Jesus was called Immanuel when he was born (Matthew 1:23). That name means God with us. Jesus promised his disciples that he would always be with them.

*some doubted:* This could refer to Thomas ({{John 20:24-29|John 20:24–29}}). But all eleven disciples might have experienced mixed feelings of worship and doubt (see also {{Matthew 14:31|Matt 14:31}}; {{Luke 24:10-11|Luke 24:10–11}}; {{John 20:24-29|John 20:24–29}}).

The authority of Jesus comes from the power given to him by the Father (see {{Matthew 7:29|Matthew 7:29}}; {{Matthew 9:6-8|9:6–8}}; {{Matthew 21:23-27|21:23–27}}; {{Matthew 26:64|26:64}}; {{John 3:35|John 3:35}}).

- *go and *(literally *going*): This is a command to make disciples. Matthew likely meant "go" as a separate command, not just as "while you go"(compare similar uses in {{Matthew 9:6|Matthew 9:6}}; {{Acts 10:20|Acts 10:20}}). 

- *make disciples*: A *disciple* turns from sin, trusts Jesus for salvation, and obeys his teachings. 

- *all nations:* The gospel mission to non-Jewish (Gentile) people officially started here (see {{Matthew 10:5-6|Matthew 10:5–6}}; {{Matthew 15:24|15:24}}; also {{Matthew 1:1|1:1}}; {{Matthew 2:1-12|2:1–12}}; {{Matthew 8:5-13|8:5–13}}; {{Matthew 21:43|21:43}}; {{Matthew 24:14|24:14}}; {{Matthew 26:13|26:13}}). 

- Two parts of making disciples are baptizing and teaching ({{Matthew 28:20|Matthew 28:20}}). Baptism is a public identification with Jesus and submission to him and his work of salvation (see {{Matthew 3:13-17|3:13–17}}; {{Matthew 10:32-33|10:32–33}}; {{Matthew 20:28|20:28}}; {{Matthew 26:28|26:28}}; {{Acts 2:38|Acts 2:38}}; {{Romans 6:1-11|Romans 6:1–11}}; {{1 Peter 3:21|1 Peter 3:21}}). 

- *in the name of:* This means entering a relationship and its benefits for true believers in Christ. 

- *Father … Son … Holy Spirit:* This phrase shows the Christian belief that the one God is three persons (Father, Son, and Holy Spirit) known as the Trinity (see also {{1 Corinthians 12:4-6|1 Corinthians 12:4–6}}; {{2 Corinthians 13:14|2 Corinthians 13:14}}; {{Ephesians 4:4-6|Ephesians 4:4–6}}; {{2 Thessalonians 2:13-14|2 Thessalonians 2:13–14}}; {{1 Peter 1:2|1 Peter 1:2}}; {{Revelation 1:4-6|Revelation 1:4–6}}).

*teaching: *The disciples are to teach people everything Jesus commanded, such as the Sermon on the Mount (chapters {{Matthew 5:1-7:29|5–7}}). People should recognize the church because it obeys the commands of Jesus ({{Matthew 5:17-20|5:17–20}}; {{Matthew 7:13-27|7:13–27}}). The authority and presence of Jesus establish the mission of the disciples (see also {{Matthew 1:23|1:23}}; {{Matthew 18:20|18:20}}).
